overview: This atlas label covers parts of western India and the Deccan in 323-200 BCE, not one empire or one religion. A northwestern outline disappears at 300 BCE; the Deccan outline remains. It includes places where Ashoka later left imperial edicts, so it cannot show uninterrupted independence. Local communities, assemblies, kingdoms and expanding imperial authority need separate histories.

periods.title: Regional societies and widening kingdoms
periods.summary: Different forms of government existed across ancient South Asia; the atlas’s collective label does not identify every local constitution.

periods.title: Imperial messages in the Deccan
periods.summary: Third-century BCE inscriptions place Mauryan authority within the retained outline. Local life continued through wider political change.

periods.title: Later regional institutions
periods.summary: Bhattiprolu’s inscriptions straddle the map cutoff; Kanaganahalli’s surviving decorated stupa belongs largely to later Satavahana centuries.

items.text: Some early states called ganas or sanghas shared power among groups of men, often styled rajas. Historians describe these as oligarchies. The label “republic” does not establish universal voting rights, and evidence for northern assemblies cannot identify the government of every Deccan settlement.

At Brahmagiri, Ashoka’s message passes through the prince and senior officers at Suvarnagiri to officials at Isila. An inscription therefore preserves an administrative chain, not just a king’s slogan. This third-century BCE evidence sits inside the atlas’s supposed kingdoms-and-republics outline.

Maski’s inscription became especially important because it names Ashoka himself. Mining engineer C. Beadon encountered it in 1915 while prospecting for gold. A search for one kind of treasure helped recover another: a named ruler’s message cut into a boulder.

Surveyors at Maski found a change from several smaller Iron Age settlements to a large Early Historic settlement covering about 15 hectares. This broader phase begins around 300 BCE and lasts well beyond the card’s end. The pattern suggests people concentrated into fewer, larger communities; it is not an exact census for 250 BCE.

Near Maski, rock surfaces used to process gold ore contain grinding hollows and deeper collection receptacles. Ashoka’s edict stands near a route toward this working area. Researchers suggest imperial interest in the gold, but proximity alone cannot prove that the emperor owned the mine or managed every worker.

Studies of the interior Deccan describe farming cereals and pulses alongside keeping cattle, sheep and goats. Fields and herds supported one another in these regional economies. This is the long-term background to the early historic settlements, rather than evidence for one standard meal served in every home.

Scattered artifacts across clay-rich fields around Maski have been interpreted as evidence for manuring in the Iron Age or Early Historic period. Household refuse carried out to fields can leave tiny traces over a wide area. Archaeologists therefore look beyond impressive monuments to understand farming and the reuse of everyday waste.

Stone-built memorials also formed part of these landscapes. Their shapes varied, and building them continued across several archaeological periods. Researchers argue that making monuments and gathering around them helped establish community ties. Their interpretation concerns shared labor and remembrance, rather than treating every large grave as a clearly identified king’s tomb.

At Girnar, later inscriptions remember a reservoir made under Chandragupta’s governor Pushyagupta and improved under Ashoka. This western place lies in the atlas’s first outline. The account shows how later rulers linked water management with earlier royal service; it is retrospective testimony, not a building receipt surviving from Chandragupta’s lifetime.

Bhattiprolu’s Buddhist relic-casket inscriptions name a ruler, Kubhiraka, alongside organized groups. ASI dates them broadly to the third or second century BCE, possibly beyond this card’s endpoint. Their language is Prakrit in a southern form of Brahmi. A distinctive script does not make the language Telugu.

One Bhattiprolu casket record brings a family into view: Kura and his parents contributed to containers for Buddhist relics. Stone receptacles protected smaller precious containers. Remembering donors in writing connected family resources, specialist craft and a religious community. The record does not reveal the family’s full wealth or everyday household arrangements.

sections.title: A writer’s name and surviving voices

items.text: At Brahmagiri, the Prakrit words Chapaḍena likhite mean “written by Chapada.” This is a modern scholarly transliteration of a third-century BCE Brahmi inscription. The accompanying word for the scribe uses Kharoshthi. Two scripts appear in one record; they do not establish that every resident spoke two languages.

A modern experiment copied Ashokan lettering with different chisels, then compared its marks with Karnataka inscriptions. Tool wear and sharpening changed the widths of lines. Writing a message on rock required physical craft as well as words: unlike a page, the boulder offered no easy eraser. The experiment tests possibilities, not one proven ancient toolkit.

Ashoka’s Brahmagiri message urges respect for parents and elders, truthfulness and compassion toward animals. These instructions bring family conduct into a public inscription. They tell us what the ruler wanted people to do; they cannot measure how kindly every household actually behaved.

Later Buddhist communities at Kanaganahalli near Sannati carved limestone stories and royal figures, including a labeled Ashoka. The surviving reliefs date from the first century BCE to the third century CE. They show his later remembrance, not a portrait carved during his reign. Buddhism and regional patronage continued after this map label stopped.

ending.text: The 200 BCE cutoff marks no collective fall. Mauryan involvement preceded it; later Satavahana patronage shaped Kanaganahalli. Regional communities and their varied traditions continued.
